definition: A full backup copies everything selected. An incremental backup copies what changed since the last backup of any kind. A differential backup copies what changed since the last full backup.
example: A full backup runs on Sunday. With incrementals, a Thursday restore needs Sunday's full plus Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday's incrementals; with differentials it needs only Sunday's full plus Wednesday's differential.
keyPoints: Full: slowest and largest to make, simplest to restore
Incremental: fastest and smallest each day, slowest restore (full plus every incremental in order)
Differential: grows each day until the next full, restore needs only the full plus the latest differential
Mixes are common, such as a weekly full with nightly differentials
Backups are still needed alongside high availability, since corrupted data is copied to every redundant system

definition: Fault tolerance is the ability of a system to keep running correctly while one or more of its parts fail, with no interruption. High availability is the wider goal of keeping a service up nearly all the time through redundancy and failover, which may allow a short interruption while a backup takes over.
example: A RAID 1 mirror keeps a server running unchanged when one disk dies (fault tolerance); a database cluster that switches to a standby node within seconds after the main node crashes gives high availability.
keyPoints: Fault tolerance aims for zero interruption when a part fails
High availability is measured in uptime, for example 99.999 percent (five nines), and may include a brief failover
Both rely on redundancy and removing single points of failure
Neither replaces backups: corruption or ransomware spreads to every copy
